query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal‐element alloys used at high temperatures, the oxidation resistance and overall material integrity are governed by which elements preferentially oxidize to form a continuous, protective scale. Specifically, when elements with the highest oxygen affinity (e.g., Cr or Al) oxidize and produce adherent, slow‐growing oxides, they block oxygen ingress and preserve the bulk alloy. In contrast, elements like Mn tend to form non‐protective, easily spalling oxides that deplete the alloy and degrade its integrity. Nanoscale chemical ordering (or local chemical heterogeneities) may further mediate which elements dominate the oxide scale. Thus, controlling the relative diffusion and oxidation kinetics of these elements can be used to enhance overall oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous multiprincipal‐element alloy (for example, equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi) that forms a single solid-solution phase
generation.intervention: Either adjust the composition (for instance, by reducing the Mn content and/or increasing Cr/Al content) or use processing methods that promote nanoscale ordering to bias the surface composition toward elements that form protective oxides
generation.conditions: Sustained high-temperature oxidizing environments (approximately 750 °C to 1300 °C) in air
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale derived from selective oxidation of high oxygen-affinity elements, mediated by local chemical order (such as grain boundary or nanoscale segregation effects) that help stabilize the protective oxide
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, different constituent elements diffuse at different rates and have distinct oxygen affinities. High-oxygen-affinity elements (Cr, Al) preferentially oxidize to form compact oxides (chromia, alumina) that act as barriers against further oxygen ingress. Conversely, reactive but more rapidly diffusing elements like Mn form non-protective oxides that spall off, depleting the alloy. Promoting a microstructure that favors the formation and retention of protective oxides over nonprotective ones thereby improves oxidation resistance and mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with a baseline multiprincipal‐element alloy that exhibits Mn-driven, non-protective oxidation, the modified alloy (with reduced Mn and/or enhanced Cr/Al and nanoscale ordering) is predicted to show a lower oxidation rate (i.e., reduced mass gain due to oxidation) and maintained or improved mechanical integrity after prolonged high-temperature exposure, as evidenced by the formation of a continuous protective oxide scale.
generation.baseline: The standard multiprincipal‐element alloy (e.g., equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi) that forms mainly non-protective oxides (due to the dominant oxidation of Mn) leading to rapid degradation of material integrity under high-temperature oxidation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold within the high-temperature range (750–1300 °C) in conventional air/oxidative environments. It may not be valid in environments with non-oxidative media or where other corrosion mechanisms dominate (e.g., molten salts with different solubility characteristics).
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of selective oxidation is supported, the precise quantitative contributions of elemental diffusion and local chemical ordering, as well as the effect of processing-induced nanostructural changes, remain to be fully calibrated. Variation in processing routes and additional environmental factors may also affect the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloy samples: one with the baseline composition (e.g., equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi) and a modified alloy that has a reduced Mn content and enhanced Cr/Al levels or has undergone a heat-treatment to promote nanoscale chemical ordering. Expose both sample sets to isothermal oxidation at 800 °C in air for 100 hours.
measurements: Thermogravimetric analysis to quantify mass gain (oxidation rate)
In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy to examine oxide scale formation and continuity
Post-oxidation mechanical testing to evaluate material integrity (e.g., microhardness or tensile properties)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate and does not form a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale (with maintained or improved mechanical integrity) relative to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis that selective oxidation governed by elemental diffusion and local chemical ordering is the mechanism driving enhanced oxidation resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. To develop and design new alloy materials with lightweight and superior comprehensive performance. In this study, a MgAlTiVFeCo lightweight high-entropy alloy (LW-HEA) was fabricated via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS) to investigate the effects of sintering temperature on its phase structure, microstructure, densification, microhardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance, and corrosion resistance. The results indicate that the ball-milled MgAlTiVFeCo LW-HEA formed a simple solid solution phase with a BCC structure. After spark plasma sintering, the phase structure of the alloy changed, maintaining the BCC phase as the primary phase while accompanying the precipitation of secondary phases. When the sintering temperature reached 1000 °C, the alloy achieved a densification of 96.7% and a microhardness of 1235.5 HV. Its hardness value is comparable to the typical range of cemented carbides, demonstrating outstanding mechanical properties.
